parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A quantity has units N s² m⁻¹. By considering force divided by acceleration, which physical quantity could it represent?

A. Acceleration
B. Force
C. Mass
D. Momentum

answer.text: C. N/(m s⁻²) = N s² m⁻¹. Since F/a = m, the quantity can be mass.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Which statement describes the weight of an object?

A. Its mass multiplied by its actual acceleration.
B. The resultant force when it falls at terminal velocity.
C. The force on it due to a gravitational field.
D. The property that resists a change in motion.

answer.text: C. Weight is gravitational force. At terminal velocity weight is still present, although the resultant force is zero.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Which statement correctly gives the principle of conservation of momentum?

A. Momentum is constant in every elastic collision, regardless of external forces.
B. Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
C. Force equals the rate of change of momentum.
D. The total momentum of an isolated system remains constant.

answer.text: D. An isolated system has no resultant external impulse, so its total momentum does not change.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A skydiver is initially at terminal speed. Immediately after her parachute opens she has her greatest upward acceleration; its magnitude then decreases until she reaches a lower terminal speed. Compare times t₁ before opening, t₂ just after opening and t₃ at the new terminal speed. Which statements are correct?

1. Acceleration magnitude is greatest at t₂.
2. Drag has the same magnitude at t₁ and t₃.
3. Drag is greatest at t₁.

A. 1 and 2
B. 1 and 3
C. 2 only
D. 3 only

answer.text: A. At either terminal speed, drag equals weight. During upward acceleration just after opening, drag exceeds weight and is greatest at t₂.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Two blocks approach each other and collide elastically in one dimension. Afterwards P moves left at 70 cm s⁻¹ and Q moves right at 20 cm s⁻¹. For such a collision, the relative approach speed equals the relative separation speed. Which pair of initial velocities is possible?

A. P: 10 cm s⁻¹ right; Q: 60 cm s⁻¹ left
B. P: 50 cm s⁻¹ right; Q: at rest
C. P: 20 cm s⁻¹ left; Q: 70 cm s⁻¹ right
D. P: 60 cm s⁻¹ right; Q: 30 cm s⁻¹ left

answer.text: D. The separation speed is 70 + 20 = 90 cm s⁻¹. Only D describes approaching blocks with this relative speed.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A solid object is fully submerged in the same liquid on Earth and on Mars. Its volume and the liquid density are unchanged. The gravitational field strengths are 9.81 N kg⁻¹ and 3.7 N kg⁻¹ respectively. What is the ratio of upthrust on Mars to upthrust on Earth?

A. 0.38
B. 1.0
C. 2.7
D. 3.6

answer.text: A. Upthrust is ρVg, so U_M/U_E = 3.7/9.81 ≈ 0.38.

parts.display_text:
A platform rests on a vertical spring. Adding a box shortens the spring by a distance x. What term describes this shortening?

A. Compression
B. Load
C. Fractional change in length
D. Force per unit area

answer.text: A. Compression is a decrease in length. The distance x is the amount by which the spring is compressed.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Model Earth as a sphere of radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m rotating once in 24 hours. Cambridge is at latitude 52.2° north. It moves in a circle parallel to the equator.

(a) Show that the radius of this circle is about 3.90 × 10⁶ m.
(b) Calculate Cambridge’s speed due to Earth’s rotation.

answer.text:
(a) The perpendicular distance to the rotation axis is r = R cos 52.2° = 3.90 × 10⁶ m.
(b) T = 24 × 3600 = 86 400 s. Therefore v = 2πr/T = 2.84 × 10² m s⁻¹, or 280 m s⁻¹ to two significant figures.

evidence.review: Source question, official answer and adapted solution checked individually.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A 58.6 kg student stands on Earth at Cambridge, latitude 52.2° north. Earth’s rotation carries her at 280 m s⁻¹ in a horizontal circle of radius 3.90 × 10⁶ m centred on the rotation axis. Treat Earth as spherical.

(a) Calculate the magnitude of her resultant force.
(b) State its direction.
(c) Sketch and label her weight and the total contact force from the ground. Explain how their vector sum gives the required resultant.

answer.text:
(a) F = mv²/r = 58.6 × 280²/(3.90 × 10⁶) = 1.18 N ≈ 1.2 N.
(b) Towards the centre of her latitude circle: perpendicular to and towards Earth’s rotation axis, not towards Earth’s centre.
(c) Weight points towards Earth’s centre. The total ground contact force points generally outwards, tilted slightly towards the pole relative to the outward radial direction. Its sum with weight points towards the rotation axis. The contact force combines the normal reaction and static friction.

A rocket ejects 90 kg of exhaust per second at 190 m s⁻¹ relative to the rocket. What thrust acts on it because of this ejection?

A. 2.1 kN
B. 17 kN
C. 18 kN
D. 162 kN

answer.text: B. Thrust equals the exhaust momentum flow rate: F = (dm/dt)v_rel = 90 × 190 = 17 100 N ≈ 17 kN.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Two bodies collide elastically in an isolated system. Which statement is incompatible with this collision?

A. In a one-dimensional collision, their relative approach and separation speeds are equal.
B. Their total kinetic energy is conserved.
C. Their total kinetic energy decreases.
D. Their total linear momentum is conserved.

answer.text: C. An elastic collision conserves total kinetic energy as well as total momentum. A decrease in the system’s kinetic energy would make the collision inelastic.

A bicycle’s back wheel pushes backwards on the road. Which force is its Newton’s-third-law partner?

A. The cyclist’s force on the pedals
B. The road’s forward force on the back wheel
C. The tension in the chain
D. The total drag on the bicycle

answer.text: B. The partner is the force exerted by the road on the back wheel. The pair acts between the same two interacting bodies in opposite directions.

A stone is released from rest and falls through air, eventually approaching terminal speed. Take downwards as positive. Which acceleration–time graph could describe this?

A. Graph A
B. Graph B
C. Graph C
D. Graph D

answer.text: D. Initially drag is negligible and acceleration is approximately g. As speed rises, drag increases and the downward resultant decreases, so acceleration tends smoothly towards zero.

parts.label: whole

A cart moves horizontally with negligible resistance. A rock with no initial horizontal velocity is dropped into it and stays inside. Compared with the empty cart immediately before impact, how do the combined cart-and-rock horizontal momentum and horizontal kinetic energy compare immediately afterwards?

A. Both are smaller
B. Momentum is smaller; kinetic energy is unchanged
C. Momentum is unchanged; kinetic energy is smaller
D. Both are unchanged

answer.text: C. No horizontal external impulse acts, so horizontal momentum is conserved. The moving mass increases; with fixed p, the horizontal kinetic energy p²/(2M) decreases.

A wooden block of mass m and volume V is fully submerged in water of density ρ. A string from the block to the bottom of the container holds it stationary. What is the string tension?

A. ρgV
B. mg + ρgV
C. mg
D. ρgV − mg

answer.text: D. Upthrust acts upwards; weight and tension act downwards. Equilibrium gives ρgV = mg + T, hence T = ρgV − mg.

A car has constant acceleration 24 cm s⁻² under a resultant force of 300 N. What is its mass, to two significant figures?

A. 13 kg
B. 1000 kg
C. 1300 kg
D. 10 000 kg

answer.text: C. Convert acceleration: 24 cm s⁻² = 0.24 m s⁻². Then m = F/a = 300/0.24 = 1250 kg ≈ 1300 kg.

parts.display_text:
An astronaut of mass m has gravitational weight mg on a launchpad. During the first instant of an upward launch the spacecraft accelerates at 0.2g; the local gravitational field is effectively unchanged. What is the gravitational force on the astronaut?

A. 1.2mg
B. mg
C. 0.8mg
D. 0

answer.text: B. The gravitational force remains mg. The upward support force must be 1.2mg, giving a resultant upward force 0.2mg, but that support force is not the weight.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
An object is fully submerged in a liquid. Which single change doubles the ratio of buoyant force to the object’s weight?

A. Double the liquid density, with the same object fully submerged.
B. Halve the object volume while keeping its density unchanged.
C. Double the object density while keeping its volume unchanged.
D. Double the object volume while keeping its density unchanged.

answer.text: A. F_b/W = ρ_liquid Vg/(ρ_object Vg) = ρ_liquid/ρ_object. Doubling the liquid density doubles the ratio; changing object volume alone cancels out.

evidence.review: Source question, official answer and adapted solution checked individually.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A wire undergoes elastic deformation when a tensile force stretches it. What does “elastic” mean here?

A. Its extension must be proportional to tensile force.
B. Its extension must not be proportional to tensile force.
C. It remains longer after the tensile force is removed.
D. It returns to its original length when the tensile force is removed.

answer.text: D. Elastic deformation is reversible: removing the deforming force restores the original length. Proportional force and extension describe the additional condition of Hooke’s law.

evidence.review: Source question, official answer and adapted solution checked individually.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
An isolated object initially at rest separates into two fragments. One has mass m and speed v. The other has mass (A − 1)m and speed u in the opposite direction, with A > 1. What relation follows from conservation of momentum?

A. v = (A/4 − 1)u
B. v = (A − 1)u
C. v = Au
D. v = (A + 1)u

answer.text: B. Initial momentum is zero. Taking the first fragment’s direction as positive gives mv − (A − 1)mu = 0, hence v = (A − 1)u.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A ball moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle on the frictionless inside surface of a cone. The cone’s side is inclined at 52° to the horizontal; the diagram is a vertical cross-section. The circular path has radius 0.15 m. Use g = 9.81 m s⁻².

(a) Draw and label the two forces on the ball.
(b) Explain why their resultant is centripetal.
(c) Calculate the ball’s speed and angular speed.
(d) Explain why a greater constant speed requires a larger circular-path radius.

answer.text:
(a) Draw weight mg vertically downward and the normal contact force perpendicular to the cone, directed inward and upward.
(b) Vertical balance gives N cos 52° = mg. The horizontal component N sin 52° supplies the inward resultant mv²/r.
(c) Dividing gives v²/r = g tan 52°. Thus v = √(0.15 × 9.81 tan 52°) = 1.37 m s⁻¹ ≈ 1.4 m s⁻¹. Angular speed ω = v/r ≈ 9.1 rad s⁻¹ using the unrounded speed; using the stated rounded 1.4 m s⁻¹ gives 9.3 rad s⁻¹.
(d) g tan 52° is fixed, so v²/r is fixed and r is proportional to v².

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A narrow beam of particles arrives normally at a stationary surface at a rate of 3.2 × 10¹⁶ particles per second. Each arriving particle has momentum magnitude 1.05 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹. Half are absorbed and half are reflected directly backwards with unchanged momentum magnitude. Determine the average force exerted on the surface.

answer.text: Each absorbed particle transfers momentum p to the surface, while each reflected particle transfers 2p. The mean transfer per particle is (p + 2p)/2 = 1.5p. Force equals momentum transferred per second: F = 1.5 × 1.05 × 10⁻²⁷ × 3.2 × 10¹⁶ = 5.04 × 10⁻¹¹ N ≈ 5.0 × 10⁻¹¹ N, in the incoming beam direction.

answer.text: C. From impulse, Ft = Δp = mv. Thus t = (8.4×10⁷×16.4)/(9.20×10⁵) = 1.50×10³ s = 25.0 min.

answer.text: C. In C, the two equal diagonal forces have vertical components that cancel; their rightward components add to balance the leftward force. A and B retain an upward resultant. In D the upward arrow exceeds the downward component of the shorter diagonal force, so its vertical resultant is nonzero.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A student investigates small metal balls falling from rest through a liquid. It is suggested that terminal velocity v=(ρ−σ)gd²/(18K), where d is sphere diameter, ρ is metal density, σ is liquid density, g=9.81 m s⁻² and K is constant. Describe, with a labelled diagram, a safe experiment to test the v–d relationship and determine K.

answer.text: Secure a tall transparent liquid column in a tray. The labelled diagram should show a sphere released at the surface, an upper timing mark well below the surface, a lower timing mark, and measured separation L between the marks; a camera or observer records passage times. Measure each sphere diameter d repeatedly in different orientations with a micrometer. Verify terminal motion by comparing speeds across successive equal-distance intervals; move the timing region lower if necessary. Time passage between the marks, repeat, and calculate v=L/t. Repeat for several diameters of the same metal, keeping liquid temperature fixed. Determine metal density by weighing spheres and dividing mass by volume πd³/6, or use an independently known density. Determine liquid density from its mass in a known-volume measuring cylinder, subtracting the empty-cylinder mass. Plot v against d². A straight line through the origin supports the model. If gradient is G, K=(ρ−σ)g/(18G). Keep the column stable, use a tray for spills and retrieve balls with a tool rather than tipping a tall filled cylinder.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Explain why the momentum of a ball changes while it travels from a hand to the ground with negligible air resistance.

answer.text: Gravity provides a nonzero resultant force. Since F = dp/dt, the ball receives a downward impulse and its vertical momentum changes continuously. Equivalently, momentum p = mv is a vector and the ball’s velocity changes in magnitude and direction.

answer.text: Use callipers. Extension x = 54.9−22.2 = 32.7 mm; absolute uncertainties add, giving ±0.2 mm. Two identical springs in series have k_eq = k/2 = 18 N m⁻¹. At equilibrium Mg=k_eqx, so M=18(0.0327)/9.81=0.060 kg to two significant figures.

What is meant by the mass and by the weight of an object on Earth?

A. Mass: momentum divided by velocity; weight: work done in lifting it one metre
B. Mass: gravitational force on it; weight: property that resists acceleration
C. Mass: pull of Earth on it; weight: mass divided by acceleration of free fall
D. Mass: property that resists acceleration; weight: pull of Earth on it

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Spheres X and Y form an isolated system. Y is heavier and initially stationary. X approaches with speed u and collides elastically with Y. Which statement must be correct?

A. X rebounds faster than u; Y moves slower than u
B. X rebounds slower than u; Y moves slower than u
C. X rebounds with speed u; Y remains stationary
D. X stops; Y moves slower than u

answer.text:
Official key B checked; editorial worked explanation:

B. In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. A is impossible because X alone would leave with more kinetic energy than it brought in. In C, X reverses while Y remains stationary, so total momentum reverses and is not conserved. For D, momentum would give vY = (mX/mY)u; the final-to-initial kinetic-energy ratio would then be mX/mY < 1, contradicting elasticity. The remaining consistent outcome is B.

A 0.10 kg ball approaches a stationary vertical bat at 20 m s⁻¹ and rebounds in the opposite direction at 15 m s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of its change in momentum?

C. 1.5 N s

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
Which statement about collisions is correct?

A. Kinetic energy is conserved in all collisions.
B. Momentum is only conserved in perfectly elastic collisions.
C. Relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation for perfectly elastic collisions.
D. Objects of different masses exert forces of different magnitudes on each other.

answer.text:
Published key C checked; editorial worked explanation:

C. In a perfectly elastic one-dimensional collision, the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach. A is false because kinetic energy is not conserved in inelastic collisions. B is false because total momentum is conserved for any isolated collision. D is false by Newton’s third law: the interaction forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

answer.text:
Published key B checked; editorial worked explanation:

B. In each equilibrium arrangement, the two string forces on the nail have a vertical resultant equal to the same picture weight, so R₁=R₂. The shorter loop in diagram 1 makes each string section more nearly horizontal. A smaller vertical component per unit tension therefore requires a larger tension: T₁>T₂.

parts.display_text: A floating sphere of weight 5.00 N supports a probe and string of combined weight 2.00 N. Seawater density is 1.03×10³ kg m⁻³, and upthrust on the probe and string is negligible. Find the submerged sphere volume.

answer.text:
Published key D checked; editorial worked explanation:

D. Vertical equilibrium requires the sphere’s upthrust to support the total 7.00 N weight. Using Fᵦ=ρgV, V=7.00/[(1.03×10³)(9.81)]=6.93×10⁻⁴ m³.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A picture of weight W hangs symmetrically from a cable. Each side has tension T and makes angle θ to the vertical. Which expression is correct? A. W=Tcosθ  B. W=2Tcosθ  C. W=Tsinθ  D. W=2Tsinθ

answer.text: Official answer B. Editorial worked explanation: Each tension contributes an upward vertical component Tcosθ because θ is measured from the vertical. Horizontal components cancel, and equilibrium gives W=Tcosθ+Tcosθ=2Tcosθ.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Only two forces X and Y act on an object in equilibrium. Which statements must be correct? 1. X and Y are equal and opposite. 2. They form a Newton’s third-law pair. 3. The object is at rest. A. only 1  B. 1 and 2  C. 1 and 3  D. 1,2 and3

answer.text: Official answer A. Editorial worked explanation: Equilibrium requires zero resultant, so two forces on the same object must be equal and opposite. Third-law pairs act on different objects, so statement 2 is false. Equilibrium may be static or constant-velocity motion, so statement 3 is not required.

answer.text: Official markscheme result: k=4000 N m⁻¹. Editorial worked explanation: The gradient is k=ΔF/Δx. Using 10.0 N at 2.5 mm, k=10.0/(2.5×10⁻³)=4.00×10³ N m⁻¹.

parts.display_text: A 0.058 kg ball hits a wall normally at 7.2 m s⁻¹, remains in contact for 52 ms, and rebounds normally at 3.6 m s⁻¹. Calculate the average force magnitude exerted by the wall.

answer.text: Official markscheme result: 12 N. Editorial worked explanation: Taking motion toward the wall as positive, u=+7.2 and v=−3.6 m s⁻¹. Thus |Δp|=m|v−u|=0.058(10.8)=0.6264 kg m s⁻¹. The average force is |Δp|/Δt=0.6264/0.052=12.05 N≈12 N.
answer.evidence: OCR H156/01 June 2023 markscheme checked on PDF page 15; editorial explanation independently recalculated.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A soil scientist puts a small soil sample in a tall glass cylinder of water. A known-frame-rate video records a particle beside a measured-distance scale. Its cumulative distances at 0.0–0.5 s are 0.0,1.2,3.5,6.2,8.9,11.6 cm at 0.1 s intervals. (a) Explain why video timing is preferable to a stopwatch. (b) State one other precaution. (c) Show terminal speed is about 0.3 m s⁻¹. (d) Use the supplied terminal-speed expression and size ranges to classify the particle.

answer.text: Official markscheme results: video reduces timing uncertainty; avoid parallax; terminal speed≈0.27 m s⁻¹; diameter≈1.0 mm, so sand. Editorial worked explanation: The intervals are only 0.1 s, comparable with human reaction time; frame-by-frame replay gives finer, repeatable timing. View the scale perpendicularly to avoid parallax. From 0.2 s onward each 0.1 s interval adds 2.7 cm, so v=0.027/0.1=0.27 m s⁻¹ and is constant. Rearranging v=2r²g(ρs−ρw)/(9η), r=√[9ηv/(2g(ρs−ρw))]=√[(9)(1.0×10⁻³)(0.27)/(2(9.81)(500))]=4.98×10⁻⁴ m. Thus diameter 2r=9.96×10⁻⁴ m≈1.0 mm, within the 0.05–2.0 mm sand range.
answer.evidence: OCR H156/01 June 2023 markscheme checked on PDF page 16; editorial explanation independently recalculated.

parts.given_text: For part (d), use v=2r²g(ρs−ρw)/(9η), with ρw=1000 kg m⁻³, ρs=1500 kg m⁻³, η=1.0×10⁻³ Pa s and g=9.81 m s⁻². Diameter ranges: clay <0.002 mm; silt 0.002–0.05 mm; sand 0.05–2.0 mm; gravel >2.0 mm.

parts.display_text:
An object moves in a straight line and a momentum–time graph is plotted. Which quantities can be calculated from the graph gradient and area?

A. Gradient: power; area: mass × displacement
B. Gradient: force; area: work done × time
C. Gradient: power; area: work done × time
D. Gradient: force; area: mass × displacement

answer.text:
Published key D checked; editorial worked explanation:

D. The gradient is dp/dt, which is the resultant force. For constant mass, the area is ∫p dt=m∫v dt=mΔx, so it equals mass × displacement.

A sphere of mass m falls with speed v. Its resistive force is kv, where k is constant. What is its terminal speed?

A. mg/k
B. km/g
C. kmg
D. k/(mg)

answer.text:
Published key A checked; editorial worked explanation:

A. At terminal speed the acceleration is zero, so the upward resistive force equals the weight: kvₜ=mg. Therefore vₜ=mg/k.

parts.display_text:
A trolley moves down a slope with constant acceleration. Its mass is doubled and it moves down the same slope again. Air resistance and friction are negligible. Which statement is correct?

A. The accelerating force is unchanged.
B. The accelerating force is halved.
C. The acceleration is unchanged.
D. The acceleration is halved.

answer.text:
Published key C checked; editorial worked explanation:

C. Along the slope the accelerating component of weight is mg sinθ. Doubling m doubles this force, but a=F/m=(mg sinθ)/m=g sinθ, so the acceleration is unchanged.

A variable force F acts on a 2.0 kg object initially at rest. The force–time graph shown has F=10 N from 0 to 0.5 s and F=20 N from 0.5 to 1.0 s. What is the speed at 1.0 s?

A. 3.75 m s⁻¹
B. 5.00 m s⁻¹
C. 7.50 m s⁻¹
D. 15.0 m s⁻¹

answer.text:
Published key C checked; editorial worked explanation:

C. The impulse is the graph area: J=10(0.5)+20(0.5)=15 N s. Since J=Δp=mv for an object starting from rest, v=15/2.0=7.50 m s⁻¹.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A heavy cable hangs from a fixed support at J and carries a load at its lower end K, as shown. The cable weight is not negligible; its cross-sectional area and density are constant. For this card, use the supplied relation that tensile stress is proportional to tension. Which graph A–D shows tensile stress σ against distance d from J to K?

answer.text:
Published key D checked; editorial worked explanation:

D. At any point the tension supports the load plus the cable below that point. Moving downward from J to K leaves progressively less cable below, so tension decreases linearly because the cable has uniform mass per unit length. At K the load still requires a nonzero tension. With constant area, stress follows the same linear decrease to a positive value, graph D.

parts.given_text: Editorially supplied prerequisite: because the cable has constant cross-sectional area, tensile stress is proportional to tension.

parts.display_text:
Two circular discs rotate together at constant speed on a common axle and are 2.00 m apart. A pellet travelling parallel to the axle at 300 m s⁻¹ makes holes separated by 45°. Using the source’s intended smallest rotation during transit, how many revolutions does each disc complete in one second?

A. 19
B. 118
C. 740
D. 1074

answer.text:
Published key A checked; editorial worked explanation:

A. The pellet transit time is t=2.00/300=6.67×10⁻³ s. The intended angular turn is 45°=1/8 revolution, so f=(1/8)/(6.67×10⁻³)=18.75 s⁻¹, which rounds to 19 revolutions per second.

evidence.detail: AQA 7408/1 June 2023 published key A, mark-scheme PDF page 27; explanation independently authored and checked.

parts.given_text: Editorially supplied interpretation: use the smallest angular rotation, 45°, during the pellet's transit between the discs; do not add an unmentioned whole revolution.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
An aircraft of mass m banks at angle θ while moving at constant speed v in a horizontal circle of radius r, as shown. The lift force acts at angle θ to the vertical. What is tanθ?

A. gv²/r
B. rv²/g
C. rg/v²
D. v²/(rg)

answer.text:
Published key D checked; editorial worked explanation:

D. Resolve lift L vertically and horizontally. Vertical equilibrium gives L cosθ=mg. The inward component supplies centripetal force: L sinθ=mv²/r. Dividing gives tanθ=(mv²/r)/(mg)=v²/(rg).

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A boat of mass M_b can displace at most volume V_b of river water of density ρ_water. It is loaded with identical steel beams, each of density ρ_steel and volume V_steel. Derive an expression for the maximum number N of whole beams the boat can carry without exceeding its maximum displacement.

answer.text: Official scoring points; editorial worked explanation: At the limiting load, the buoyant force equals the total weight: ρ_water V_b g=(M_b+Nρ_steel V_steel)g. Cancelling g and rearranging gives the continuous capacity N_cont=(ρ_water V_b−M_b)/(ρ_steel V_steel). Because only complete beams can be loaded, the physical maximum is N_max=⌊N_cont⌋. The stated feasibility condition makes N_cont non-negative; otherwise the empty boat itself would already exceed the specified displacement capacity.
answer.evidence: 2018 AP Physics 2 scoring guidelines, Question 4, PDF page 12; official points and editorial explanation independently checked.

parts.given_text: Assume ρ_water V_b ≥ M_b, so the empty boat can float without exceeding its maximum displaced volume.
